highlights.text: Omand held no special hatred for the non-people. He cared about them as much as he did anyone else…as in, not at all. Arranging their genocide had been nothing personal. It had simply been something that had been necessary to satisfy the deal he had made with a sea demon.
People are the same as dogs. They must be trained to be obedient. Punish wickedness. Reward devotion. Do both publicly so the rest will learn.”

“In turning Ashok Vadal into a criminal, I envisioned a wonderful tool of destabilization and disruption. He was a good Protector, but he has been an outstanding rebel. Ashok has far outperformed the use I imagined I’d wring from him. Yet, his use to me is over. Now he vexes me by not dying when it is convenient for me. I believe I may have created a monster, Taraba.”
Who will question the need for firm leadership, while beams of scalding fire shoot from the sky, and the rebels have stolen away the very water they drink?”
Things move slowly, until they don’t. Nothing changes, until everything does.
Omand was always honest with himself. Only weak men deceived themselves into believing comforting things that were untrue. Great men dealt in cold reality.

“I decide my own Law now, Gutch.” “Ah, then I shall not worry about you suddenly decapitating me, then!” “I did not promise that.” “I’ll take what I can get.”

More murders than I can count. Probably more than even you can imagine. And none of them troubled me in the least until I was exposed to the corrupting influence of that damnable Keta, and all his talk of fate and consequences. And now all those dead haunt me. I was better off before I ever heard Keta’s words, because I was blessed by ignorance, but with wisdom I become a man condemned.

Jagdish had gone from prisoner to phontho, from looming execution to highest promotion. He had been both enemy and friend to the most dangerous man in the world and had fought his way across the continent and back, slaying demons and wizards along the way, all to redeem his name.
Fate might not be thwarted often, but she seemed to have a soft spot for those who gave their all.

“Omand wants me dead and my house in ruins. What do you want, Devedas?” “A righteous justice and a ruler wise enough to dispense it.”
“You judges have spoken in nonsense and poetry for so long that when a man who understands the true purpose of the Law tells the truth, it baffles you.
“I swear I tried to save you.” “I’ll start to believe that only if we go to the gallows at the same time, and I still won’t be convinced until I see your rope snap tight.”
“When I get condemned tomorrow, my final request will be for them to hang you first, so I can at least have the satisfaction of watching you die before I do.”

He’d killed children for his Order and his own ambitions. He would not kill children for his gods.

“I have lived my entire life trying to win the great game. I learned more about magic than anyone else has in the last few centuries. I have lied and murdered and consorted with demons. Finally, after all that the work is done and the Capitol is mine. Yet, I feel no triumph from this, Taraba. Only a yearning for more. The time for petty maneuvers is over. I do not care to defend my kingdom from the king I made for it.”

Some call him the Night Father, as he is the enemy of Mother Dawn.” “I have met her.” “I have not had that honor.” “I am unsure if it is an honor, as she is a creature of riddles.
In the prophecies of the end times, on one side there is always the Forgotten’s Warrior, Voice, and Priest, while on the other there is the Demon, the King, and the Mask.”

Grand Inquisitor Omand Vokkan spoke the secret words he’d been entrusted with by a dying god he’d once met beneath the desert sands. “Soham nava vyavastha adhisa chanakya.”
“But you’re dead. I killed you.” “You came closer than most.”

That’s what makes it even worse. You give all and ask for nothing for yourself in return. You’re the effortless living paragon of duty and justice and honor and bravery every other thing a man is supposed to aspire to be.
